chapters.title: Pick a niche and programs to promote
chapters.goal: Land on one topic you genuinely know, and 2-3 affiliate programs in it you'd recommend even without being paid.
explanation: Start from what you already know or consume a lot — gaming gear, skincare, study tools, sneakers. Real knowledge makes your content believable; faking expertise doesn't.

Search "[topic] affiliate program" and check the big networks (Amazon Associates, Impact, ShareASale, Awin) for programs in that niche — compare commission rate and cookie duration (how long after a click you still get credit).
Narrow to one niche specific enough that you can become the go-to voice in it, not "tech" but "budget mechanical keyboards for students."
Shortlist 2-3 products/programs you'd genuinely use or already do — never promote something you wouldn't personally recommend to a friend.
Write your one-sentence angle: "I help [who] choose [what] without [common frustration]."
chapters.example: Omer was already deep into budget keyboard builds for his own desk. He joined two keyboard-parts affiliate programs with decent commissions and cookie durations, and his angle became: "I help students build a great keyboard for under $60 without getting scammed by fake reviews."
mistakes: Picking the highest-commission program in a topic you don't actually care about — the content shows it, and so does the audience.
Spreading across ten unrelated niches instead of owning one.
Signing up for a program without reading its terms on prohibited promotion methods (e.g. no fake reviews, no misleading claims).
chapters.template:
Niche worksheet:
Topic I actually know: ____
Programs found (name / commission % / cookie length): ____
Why I'd recommend these even unpaid: "____"
One-sentence angle: "I help [who] [do what] without [frustration]."
checklist: Wrote down 3 topics I genuinely know well
Found and compared at least 2 affiliate programs in that niche
Read each program's terms for prohibited promotion methods
Wrote my one-sentence angle

chapters.title: Know who's actually reading or watching you
chapters.goal: Describe the exact person who'd trust your recommendation enough to click through and buy.
explanation: Your audience isn't "everyone interested in X" — it's a specific person at a specific decision point (about to buy their first keyboard, stuck choosing between two brands).
Read comments and questions on existing content in your niche — what do people keep asking that isn't clearly answered anywhere?
Notice what convinces YOU to trust a recommendation online (a real demo, an honest downside, a specific number) and build that into your content style.
Write a short buyer profile: who they are, what they're about to decide, and what would make them trust a stranger's link.
Test it — show a draft post/video to 2-3 people matching the profile and ask what would stop them from clicking.
chapters.example: Omer's profile: "A student who's outgrown their laptop keyboard, has a $50-70 budget, and is overwhelmed by conflicting YouTube reviews." His content leaned hard into honest trade-offs at that exact price point instead of hyping the most expensive option.
mistakes: Writing generic "top 10" content that could apply to anyone, convincing no one.
Ignoring the comments section, which is free research on exactly what your audience doesn't understand yet.
Never testing content on a real person before publishing.
chapters.template:
Audience one-pager:
Who: ____
What they're deciding right now: ____
What makes them trust a recommendation: "____"
Where they already hang out online: ____
checklist: Read comments/questions on 5+ pieces of existing content in my niche
Wrote the buyer profile
Identified what specifically builds trust for this audience
Tested a draft on someone matching the profile

chapters.title: Understand the commission structure
chapters.goal: Know exactly how and how much you get paid per action, so you can judge which programs are actually worth your time.
explanation: You don't set a price — the merchant does. What matters to you is the commission rate (often 3-10% on physical goods, 20-50%+ on digital products/courses) and the payout trigger (per sale, per sign-up, per free trial).
Check the cookie duration — how many days after someone clicks your link they can still buy and you get credit. Longer is better; 24 hours is weak, 30+ days is strong.
Calculate realistic numbers: if 100 people click and 2% buy a $40 item at 8% commission, that's roughly $6.40 per 100 clicks — useful for judging how much traffic you'd actually need.
Watch for a minimum payout threshold (some programs won't pay you until you've earned $50-100) and how often payouts happen.
Compare 2-3 programs on this same math before committing your content time to one.
chapters.example: Omer compared two keyboard-parts programs: one paid 5% with a 7-day cookie, the other 8% with a 30-day cookie. The second was clearly better even though the per-click math looked similar, because a keyboard purchase decision often takes people weeks.
mistakes: Chasing the highest advertised commission % without checking cookie duration or payout threshold.
Not calculating realistic expected earnings before investing weeks of content into one program.
Missing a program's minimum payout threshold and being surprised it never pays out at low volume.
chapters.template:
Commission comparison:
Program A: ____% commission, ____ day cookie, $____ minimum payout
Program B: ____% commission, ____ day cookie, $____ minimum payout
Estimated earnings per 100 clicks (using a 2% realistic conversion guess): $____
checklist: Found the commission rate for each shortlisted program
Found the cookie duration for each
Found the minimum payout threshold and frequency
Did the rough per-100-clicks math for comparison

chapters.title: Equipment and startup costs
chapters.goal: Know that this can start at $0, and know exactly what (if anything) is worth spending on early.
explanation: Affiliate marketing is one of the lowest-cost paths here — a phone and free editing apps are enough to start; the real investment is time.

The only common paid step is applying to a network that requires an existing website/following — if you're rejected for having no audience yet, build content first and reapply later rather than paying for shortcuts.
If you eventually want a simple link-in-bio page or a basic website, free tiers exist (Linktree free, a free blog platform) — don't pay for this before you have any traffic.
Avoid any paid "affiliate marketing course" promising guaranteed income — the free official documentation of each network covers everything you need to start.
If you do spend anything (a domain name, a paid tool), set a small hard cap and track it.
chapters.example: Omer spent $0 for his first three months — free editing app, free blog platform for his "best budget keyboards" list, and existing social accounts. He only bought a $12/year domain once he had steady traffic.
mistakes: Paying for a "guaranteed income" affiliate course instead of using free program documentation.
Buying tools or a custom website before having any content or traffic to justify it.
Applying to a big network before having any content, then getting discouraged by rejection instead of building first.
chapters.template:
Startup cost sheet:
Total spent so far: $____
Anything I'm considering buying: ____ — do I have traffic that justifies it yet? Yes/No
checklist: Confirmed I can start with $0 in tools
Avoided any paid "guaranteed income" course or program
If considering a paid tool, checked whether current traffic justifies it
Set a hard cap for any spending

chapters.title: Build a trustworthy voice
chapters.goal: Make your recommendations feel like they come from a real, honest person — not an ad.
explanation: Pick a consistent name/handle across the platform(s) you'll use, and a simple visual style (thumbnail style, intro line) that makes your content recognizable.
Always disclose that a link is an affiliate link, clearly and early — not buried in fine print. It's legally required in most places and it actually builds trust rather than losing it.
Include at least one honest downside in every recommendation — "this is great, but the app is clunky" — one-sided hype content converts worse and gets less trust over time.
Write a short "why trust me" note for your bio/about section: your actual experience with the niche, in one or two sentences.
Keep your tone the same whether or not a link is attached — audiences notice when enthusiasm only appears for paid links.
chapters.example: Omer's videos always opened with "budget keyboard breakdown, this link is an affiliate link, I get a small cut if you buy" — said naturally in the first few seconds, not hidden. Comments regularly thanked him for the honesty.
mistakes: Hiding or burying affiliate disclosure — it's both a trust-killer and, in most places, against advertising law.
Only ever posting glowing reviews with zero downsides.
Changing tone/enthusiasm noticeably only for sponsored or affiliate content.
chapters.template:
Brand basics:
Consistent name/handle: ____
Disclosure line I'll say/write every time: "____"
"Why trust me" bio line: "____"
checklist: Picked a consistent name/handle
Wrote a clear, early disclosure line and use it every time
Included a genuine downside in my last piece of content
Wrote a short "why trust me" bio line

chapters.title: Choose your content channel
chapters.goal: Pick one platform format to publish consistently on, matched to where your audience already is.
explanation: Match format to niche: visual/physical products often work well as short-form video; software/apps often work well as a blog post or comparison article; either can work — check where similar creators in your niche actually get engagement.
Commit to a specific, sustainable posting rhythm (e.g. 2 pieces of content a week) rather than a burst followed by silence.
Link placement matters: put your affiliate link somewhere easy to find (bio link, pinned comment, description) and mention where it is in the content itself.
Use whatever basic click tracking the program or a free link shortener gives you, so you can see which content actually drives clicks.
Repurpose one piece of content across 2 formats (a video's script becomes a blog post) instead of creating everything from scratch every time.
chapters.example: Omer picked YouTube Shorts as his primary format since keyboard builds are visual, cross-posted the same clips to TikTok and Instagram Reels, and kept his affiliate links pinned in every video's description and top comment.
mistakes: Posting on 4 platforms at once with no consistent rhythm on any of them.
Making it hard to find the link — buried in a bio with no mention of where it is.
Never checking which specific piece of content actually drove clicks.
chapters.template:
Channel plan:
Primary platform: ____
Posting rhythm: ____ pieces per week
Where the link lives: ____
How I'll check which content drives clicks: ____
checklist: Picked one primary content format/platform
Set a realistic, sustainable posting rhythm
Made the affiliate link easy to find and mentioned where it is
Set up basic click tracking

chapters.title: Land your first commission
chapters.goal: Get one real click-through purchase — proof the whole loop actually works.
explanation: Your first commission usually comes from your most specific, most helpful piece of content — not your most polished one. Answer one real question completely.
Make the recommendation feel earned: show the product in real use, not just a link dump.
Reply to every comment asking a follow-up question about the product — those replies often convert better than the original post.
Check your affiliate dashboard regularly in the first weeks so you learn which specific content and audience segment actually converts.
Don't panic if the first few weeks show clicks but no sales — for higher-cookie-duration programs, a sale can land days or weeks after the click.
chapters.example: Omer's first commission came from a comment reply — someone asked "does this switch feel mushy?", he gave a specific, honest answer with the link, and they bought two days later through the 30-day cookie window.
mistakes: Giving up after one week of clicks-but-no-sales without checking the cookie window.
Never replying to follow-up questions, which are often the actual moment of decision.
Judging success only by the most polished content instead of the most specifically helpful one.
chapters.template:
First-commission log:
Content that got the click: ____
Question or comment that led to it (if any): "____"
Days between click and sale: ____
checklist: Published at least one specific, genuinely helpful piece of content
Replied to every follow-up question
Checked the affiliate dashboard weekly
Logged the details once the first commission landed

chapters.title: Keep the audience's trust
chapters.goal: Make sure people keep clicking your links in the future because your past recommendations were honest and useful.
explanation: If a product you recommended turns out disappointing after more use, say so publicly — a follow-up correction builds more long-term trust than staying silent.
Keep disclosure consistent on every piece of content, not just the first few — audiences notice if it quietly disappears.
Don't accept every affiliate offer that comes your way — turning down a bad-fit, high-commission product protects the trust that makes the good ones convert.
Answer audience questions honestly even when the honest answer is "don't buy this, get the other one instead" — it's the single biggest trust builder in this business model.
Keep a simple list of what you've recommended so you can follow up or correct yourself later without having to remember everything.
chapters.example: When a keyboard Omer recommended developed a common defect after a few months, he posted a follow-up video about it and updated the article. Subscribers specifically mentioned that follow-up as why they kept trusting his future recommendations.
mistakes: Staying silent when a past recommendation turns out to be wrong.
Accepting every affiliate offer regardless of fit, diluting trust in all of them.
Letting disclosure quietly slip once an audience is established.
chapters.template:
Trust log:
Products recommended (running list): ____
Any follow-up corrections needed: ____
Offers turned down and why: ____
checklist: Started a running list of what I've recommended
Posted a follow-up/correction where one was needed
Kept disclosure consistent on every piece of content
Turned down at least one bad-fit offer on purpose

chapters.title: Getting paid
chapters.goal: Understand how and when commission money actually reaches you, and set it up legally.
explanation: Most affiliate networks require the account holder to be 18+ — under that age, a parent applies and holds the account, with you tracking your own content and results.
Understand the payout method (bank transfer, PayPal, check) and minimum threshold before you rely on any specific number arriving.
Payouts are often monthly and often delayed by a "clearance period" (in case of returns) — don't expect same-day money after a sale.
Keep the login and payout details agreed upon and secure between you and the account-holding parent — never shared with anyone outside that.
Watch for scam "affiliate programs" that ask YOU to pay an upfront fee to join — legitimate programs never charge you to become an affiliate.
chapters.example: Omer's father held the Amazon Associates and keyboard-parts affiliate accounts, and they agreed payouts would transfer to Omer's own savings account monthly after clearing, with Omer tracking every commission in a shared spreadsheet.
mistakes: Paying an upfront "joining fee" for an affiliate program — a clear scam signal.
Expecting instant payout without accounting for clearance periods and minimum thresholds.
Not agreeing on the payout arrangement with the account-holding parent in advance.
chapters.template:
Payment setup record:
Account holder (must be 18+ for most networks): ____
Payout method and minimum threshold: ____
Clearance/delay period: ____
Agreed transfer arrangement to me: ____
checklist: Confirmed the account holder meets each program's age requirement
Understood the payout method, threshold and clearance period
Agreed the transfer arrangement with the account-holding parent
Never paid any upfront fee to join a program
chapters.parentNote: Most affiliate networks require an 18+ account holder. A parent applying and holding the account is the standard route under that age.

chapters.title: Accounting and taxes
chapters.goal: Track every commission earned and understand what's owed, without waiting until it's confusing.
explanation: Affiliate commissions are taxable income in almost every country, same as any other business income, including for minors — the specific rules vary by country and need a real check for where you live.
Keep a simple log: date, program, amount, and payout date for every commission — most networks give you a dashboard export, use it.
Set aside a portion of every payout (a rough 20-25% placeholder is common) rather than spending all of it, until you know the real number that applies to you.
Some programs issue tax forms (in the US, a 1099 above a threshold) — know whether yours does and keep records either way.
Have one real conversation with a parent, and once income is more than pocket change, check your country's actual rules for minors' business income.
chapters.example: Omer exported his commission history monthly from each program's dashboard into one spreadsheet, and set aside a quarter of each payout into a separate account so nothing was a surprise later.
mistakes: Assuming small affiliate commissions aren't taxable — in most places they are, regardless of amount.
Not keeping records because the network "already tracks it" — dashboards can be hard to access after account changes or don't cover everything.
Spending 100% of payouts with nothing set aside.
chapters.template:
Commission log (one row per payout):
Date | Program | Amount | Payout date | Running total
Set-aside plan: ____% of each payout → $____ saved so far
checklist: Started a running commission log
Set aside a percentage of each payout
Checked whether any program issues a tax form
Had one conversation with a parent about how this income is handled
chapters.parentNote: Affiliate income is taxable in most places, including for minors, and the exact filing rules depend on your country. This needs a parent involved, and a real check with a tax authority once income is meaningful — see the Legal section in this app for country-specific starting notes.

chapters.title: Growing your affiliate income
chapters.goal: Turn one working niche and channel into a steadier, slowly-diversifying source of commission income.
explanation: Once you have consistent traffic, look at which specific content and which specific product recommendations actually convert, and make more of that pattern.
Diversify across 2-4 programs in your niche rather than depending entirely on one company's commission rates or program terms, which can change.
Consider negotiating a higher commission rate once you have proven, consistent traffic — many programs will do this for reliable affiliates, but only if you ask.
Build an owned asset over time (an email list, a resource page) that doesn't depend entirely on any one platform's algorithm.
Review monthly, not daily — total clicks, conversion rate, and earnings per 100 clicks tell you more over a month than any single viral post.
chapters.example: After six months, Omer noticed his comparison-style posts converted 3x better than his "unboxing" content. He shifted most of his effort there, added a second complementary affiliate program, and started a short email list of people wanting build guides.
mistakes: Depending on a single program that could change its terms or shut down without warning.
Never asking for a better commission rate despite having proven, consistent traffic.
Reviewing performance obsessively day to day instead of looking at real monthly trends.
chapters.template:
Monthly growth review:
Total clicks: ____  Conversions: ____  Earnings per 100 clicks: $____
Best-converting content type: ____
One thing I'm doing more of next month: ____
checklist: Identified my best-converting content pattern
Diversified into at least a second program in my niche
Considered or asked about a better commission rate
Set up a simple monthly (not daily) performance review
